transcript.content: Hello, welcome to the clinic. Can you tell me what brings you in today?

Well, doc... I guess it’s just getting to be too much. I do maintenance and repair work, mostly commercial stuff, you know, electrical panels, heavy equipment. And lately, I just... I can’t stop jumping out of my skin. I mean, literally jumping. 

Just the other day, I was down in this cramped mechanical room, and one of the younger guys drops a wrench on the concrete. Just a tool dropping, happens a hundred times a day, right? But I swear to God, I nearly went through the ceiling. Or if I'm testing a circuit and a breaker snaps—you know that loud, sharp *crack* they make when they trip? I hear that, and my whole body just violently flinches. And it’s not even just the loud noises. If I’m working, head deep in a machine, and somebody just walks up behind me to ask a question, I practically spin around ready to swing before I even realize who it is. 

And the worst part... the worst part is what happens after. Like, anyone would jump if a heavy tool hits the floor, but they just laugh and pick it up and get back to it. Me? My heart starts hammering against my ribs so hard I can feel it in my teeth. And it just keeps hammering. Long after everyone else has moved on and gone back to work, I’m still standing there, heart racing, feeling completely wired, just trying to get a grip. It’s exhausting, man. I just can't seem to settle down no matter what I do.
Do you find yourself constantly on edge or overly alert, even in situations where there’s no real danger, like when you’re at home or around family?

Yeah, I guess... I mean, "on edge" is putting it mildly, doc. It's like... it's like I'm a coiled spring, you know? Just waiting for something to snap. And it doesn't matter where I am. You'd think being at home, in my own house, with my wife and kids, that I'd be able to just... turn it off. Unwind. Have a beer, watch the game, just be a normal guy. But I can't. I'm sitting there on the couch, and my eyes are constantly darting around. I'm listening to every creak the house makes, every car that drives by outside. 

My wife, she tries to be understanding, but I know it drives her crazy. She'll be cooking dinner, and she'll drop a spoon or something, and I'm instantly out of my chair, heart pounding, looking for the threat. And she's just like, "It's just a spoon, honey." And I know it's just a spoon! My brain knows it's just a spoon, but my body... my body doesn't care. It's like my nervous system is stuck in overdrive and someone threw away the key. 

Even when I'm trying to sleep, which is a whole other joke, I'm just lying there, staring at the ceiling, analyzing every shadow. I keep the bedroom door locked, I check the windows three times before I go to bed. The kids, they come running into the room in the morning, just being kids, loud and happy, and I practically jump out of my skin before I realize it's them. It makes me feel terrible, honestly. They're just kids. They shouldn't have to tiptoe around their own dad because he's acting like a crazy person. But I just can't seem to turn off this... this radar I have going all the time. It's exhausting. I'm just so tired of being alert all the time, you know? It's like I'm fighting a war that isn't even happening.

Other previously considered disorders (e.g., Generalized Anxiety Disorder, Panic Disorder, Adjustment Disorder, and Persistent Complex Bereavement Disorder) are less consistent with the clinical presentation, particularly the pervasive state of hyperarousal and reactivity, which is central to F43.10. No further questioning is needed at this point to distinguish between these disorders.
